Read only the supplied manuscript images. Do not search for the text, open a
catalogue or edition, or consult an earlier transcription. Do not identify the
work or author. If prior context has already revealed a proposed identification
or reading, stop and report that exposure instead of calling this a blind reading.

Begin with a brief image-only layout survey. Note orientation, columns, running
titles, rubrics, enlarged initials, underlined text, and interlinear or marginal
glosses when visible. Distinguish observations from tentative interpretations
such as main text with commentary. Do not infer author, work, date, or provenance.
A tight crop may not show the layout; say so rather than guessing.

Use those features to choose a few useful spans: headings or question openings,
then connecting prose, transitions or citation chains. Keep quoted lemmata and
commentary separate. Read enough surrounding prose to make a later source match
checkable; a full transcription is not required. State which areas you selected
and which remain unread. Suggest a wider view or an adjacent crop if needed.

Transcribe those spans, preserving physical lines. Label each line with its
image filename and a line number counted from the top of that image. Keep columns
and marginal additions separate. Note overlapping crops rather than treating
repeated lines as additional text.

Retain abbreviation marks when possible. Put proposed expansions in parentheses,
uncertain readings before a question mark, and unreadable text in [illegible].
Describe visible deletions and additions explicitly. Do not supply missing words
from what would make grammatical or philosophical sense. Leave uncertainty visible.

Return the reading as UTF-8 plain text. Include limitations (cropped lines, damage,
uncertain column order) in that same response. This is an unverified image reading.

PACKET-02 - UNVERIFIED BLIND IMAGE READING

Exposure statement: My context contained general project notes (a fragment-identification
project at a monastic archive, batch names) but no proposed identification, author, work
or prior transcription for these images. I did not search or consult any edition, and
opened only PROMPT.md and the image files (directory listing only; packet.json not
opened). No identification is offered.

======================================================================
LAYOUT SURVEY
======================================================================
Overviews: image-001 (face A, pencil "Stams, STA, Frg. 144r" in left margin) and
image-008 (face B, pencil "... Frg. 144v" in right margin). Tiles: image-002/003 (face A
upper), 005/006 (face A lower), image-010/011 (face B upper), 013/014 (face B lower).
Images 004, 007, 009, 012 are almost entirely a uniform grey masking rectangle (plus a
sliver of plastic weight / background); they contain no text. A grey mask also covers
part of each overview beside the fragment; I cannot tell whether there is more parchment
beneath it.

Fragment: a vertical strip of parchment cut through a single column of text. On face A
the outer (left) margin and line-beginnings survive, text cut at right. On face B the
line-endings and outer (right) margin survive, text cut at left. About 25 lines per
face, top and bottom lines cropped. Script: a late Caroline / early Gothic book hand,
dark brown ink, red touching on capitals (face B: "Et", "Hec", "Habet"). Ruled. No
glosses. Face A: a large drawn sign ("S"/"5"-shaped, perhaps a later pen trial or
signe) in left margin beside l.9-10; faint later marginal scribbles; words "hoc loco"
underlined on l.15. Face B: "obuolu" underlined on l.15; a few small marginal ticks.
Tentative interpretation: continuous exegetical/moral prose quoting and explaining a
scriptural passage (citations of "beatus iob" and a "psalmista" are visible), not a
text-with-separate-commentary layout.

Selected spans: all legible lines on both faces. Nothing deliberately left unread;
losses are physical (column cut).

Conventions: (x) expansion; word? uncertain; [illegible]; [...] = text lost at cut edge.
Lines numbered from top of the named image, counting text lines.
